title: the words on the doorpost
hookLine: the little case on the doorframe; what's actually inside it
tomorrow: two flames, eighteen minutes before sunset

cards: That little case on the doorframe. Right side as you walk in, about shoulder height, often tilted. Some people touch it on the way out and kiss their fingertips, as quick as checking for keys.
Most people assume the case is the thing. It isn't. The case is just a case.

teach.b: Inside is a tiny scroll, written by hand on parchment by a trained scribe with a quill.

It carries a passage from the Torah that opens with six well-known words, the Shema: hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one. The same passage says to write these words on the doorposts of your house.
So people did, literally. Mezuzah is simply Hebrew for doorpost: the word for the frame became the word for the scroll.
On the back, many scribes write one of God's names, Shaddai, which some read as the initials of guardian of the doors of Israel. Now the tilt.

A well-known medieval teacher, Rashi, said hang it upright. His grandson said lay it flat. Many Ashkenazi Jews, whose families come from central and eastern Europe, hang it at a slant: a little of both.
Many Sephardi Jews hang it upright. And the touch?
Not a lucky charm; the great teacher Maimonides warned against treating it as one. It's a reminder. Every time you cross the threshold, going out or coming home, you pass the words.
And one more thing about this door: it doesn't check your beliefs or your family tree on the way in. However you got here, you're welcome to walk through.

how: Jews fix a mezuzah, a handwritten parchment of the Shema passages in a case, on the right doorpost of the doorways of the home, and many touch it and kiss their fingertips when passing through.

games.q: what's inside the case — tap the pairs.
p: upright or flat? a little of both

s: the words are. the case just protects the handwritten scroll.
the slant comes from an old disagreement
Rashi said upright, his grandson said flat. many hang it at a slant: a little of both.
a mezuzah is a good-luck charm
Maimonides warned against treating it as one. it's a reminder of the words.

games.q: you're hanging a mezuzah. Rashi said upright; his grandson said flat. what did many Ashkenazi families end up doing?
o: at a slant, a little of both.
games.why: a slant: a small monument to an argument nobody had to lose. many Sephardi Jews hang it upright.

games.q: put the mezuzah together, in order.
p: a scribe writes the words by hand
the case goes on the doorpost

practice: One breath with the bell. Rest your fingertips on the nearest doorframe, or just picture your own front door. Breathe in.
As you breathe out, think of one thing you'd like to carry through that door today. Then lift your hand.

wordCard.voice: The mezuzah. Doorpost, and the handwritten words fixed to it: hear, O Israel. First word on your strand.

orig.note: Hebrew: doorpost. the word for the frame became the word for the scroll on it.

carryVoice: Your line: take the words with you. That's what the touch on the way out means. See you tomorrow.
